channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Emerging-market data stayed broadly firm: Brazil's inflation cooled to 4.52%, setting up another rate cut, ASEAN monitor AMRO lifted Vietnam's 2026 growth forecast to 7.5%, and the OECD sees Malaysia growing about 4.9%.
item.description:
Beyond the big powers, emerging economies showed resilience. Brazilian consumer prices rose 4.52% in the year to early July, below all forecasts in a Bloomberg survey and down from 4.8%, as food and beverage prices fell — clearing the way for another central-bank rate cut and easing pressure on households. In Southeast Asia, the ASEAN+3 monitor AMRO raised Vietnam's 2026 growth forecast to 7.5% from 7.2% and trimmed its inflation outlook, with Standard Chartered even more bullish at 9.5%. The OECD's latest survey sees Malaysia growing 4.9% in 2026 and 5.0% in 2027, moderating from 5.2% but still solid, while flagging downside risks from trade tensions and higher commodity prices. Argentina, under President Milei, reported 292 export-market openings for farm and agri-industrial goods in the first half, part of a broader push praised by the IMF's chief as evidence of a "much sounder" economy.

Industry Impact

Emerging markets remain the main engine of global demand growth for chemicals, construction materials and manufactured goods, and this run of firm data supports the case for prioritising them. Cooling Brazilian inflation and likely rate cuts should revive consumption and construction; Vietnam's upgraded outlook cements its role as a manufacturing and supply-chain hub drawing investment away from China; and Malaysia's steady growth underpins regional demand. The common risk is external — trade tensions and higher commodity and oil prices from the Iran war could yet slow these economies. For suppliers, the signal is to keep building presence in resilient ASEAN and Latin American markets while hedging against the shared geopolitical and energy headwinds.

Financial Post - Canada | VIR - Vietnam Investment Review | OECD | Japan Today

item.title: India's industrial output rose 7.3% in June, a six-month high led by manufacturing and power, but a Reuters poll saw growth easing to 6.6% in the year to March 2027 as weak investment and higher oil prices bite.
item.description:
India's index of industrial production grew 7.3% year-on-year in June, a six-month high, up from 5.1% in May, driven by a 7.8% rise in manufacturing (about three-quarters of the index) and a 10.6% jump in electricity and gas supply. Yet the medium-term picture is softer: a Reuters poll of economists projects GDP growth slowing to 6.6% in the fiscal year ending March 2027, down from 7.7% the prior year, on weak private investment and higher oil prices, before edging up to 6.8% the following year. New Delhi is meanwhile courting investment and defending strategic industries: a planned INR 800 billion incentive package would cover up to half the cost of drilling exploratory wells to attract foreign money into deepwater oil and gas, and pharmaceutical exports hit a record USD 31.12 billion, underlining India's role as supplier of roughly 20% of the world's generic medicines and 60% of global vaccine demand.

Industry Impact

India remains one of the few large economies growing above 6%, a magnet for chemical, manufacturing and pharmaceutical investment even as the near-term forecast cools. The strong June output and record pharma exports confirm robust end-market demand for specialty chemicals, coatings and intermediates, while the deepwater-energy package signals New Delhi's drive to cut import dependence and build domestic feedstock and energy security. The higher-oil-and-weak-investment drag on FY27 growth is a caution, but the structural story — industrialisation, formalisation and export ambition — stays intact. For suppliers, India offers durable demand growth and localisation opportunities, provided they navigate its shifting tariff and localisation rules.

LiveMint | The Economic Times | Business Standard

item.title: The UK pledged GBP 600 million for aerospace and a modified Airbus A350 flew a record 24 hours non-stop for Qantas, while European defence sentiment brightened on strong Airbus and Thales results.
item.description:
Britain's new government unveiled a GBP 600 million aerospace package, including a GBP 100 million Aerospace Supply Chain Fund to help suppliers scale up and over GBP 500 million for research into greener flight, framed as part of UK reindustrialisation. In a headline-grabbing test, a specially modified Airbus A350-1000ULR flew 24 hours and 24 minutes non-stop from Melbourne to Toulouse, tracked by more than 3.6 million people online — a key step toward Qantas's "Project Sunrise," which from late 2027 aims to fly Sydney to London non-stop, the world's longest passenger route. Investor mood toward European defence firms is improving after solid results from Airbus and French group Thales, with French stocks leading, after months of profit-taking hit names such as Rheinmetall. The defence-industrial theme runs wider: Ukraine plans to make up to seven million small attack drones this year, and Taiwan will simulate converting civilian factories to military production in an August exercise.

Industry Impact

Aerospace and defence are high-value markets for advanced adhesives, composites, coatings and sealants, and this cluster of news points to sustained demand: government funding for supply chains and greener aircraft, record ultra-long-haul aircraft entering service, and a broad rearmament drive across Europe and Asia. Greener-flight research in particular pulls demand toward lightweight composite structures and new bonding and coating chemistries. The UK supply-chain fund and Europe's improving defence outlook suggest multi-year order visibility for qualified suppliers. Firms with aerospace-grade materials should position for both the sustainability transition and the rearmament wave, while noting the long qualification cycles and security requirements that gate entry into these programmes.

JEC Group | ABC - Australian Broadcasting Corporation | Wallstreet:online | The Economic Times

item.title: Mercedes-Benz's profit fell on a 30% China slump, yet its shares jumped up to 6% as it held its margin target, while Chinese brands press deeper into Europe and pure-electric cars hit a record 22% of EU sales.
item.description:
Mercedes-Benz reported second-quarter sales down nearly 7% to 417,865 vehicles, with car-division profit falling 26% as a 30% drop in China overwhelmed gains of 4% in Europe and 10% in the US; its car margin slipped to 4.0%. Yet the shares rose up to 6% — their highest since mid-June — because the company kept its full-year margin target, and the rally lifted BMW, Volkswagen and Porsche too. The relief sits against a structural squeeze: analysts at S&P Global Mobility now expect Chinese brands such as Chery, BYD and MG to take well above the once-forecast 20% of the European market, as fierce home competition and US tariff barriers push them toward Europe; European makers may have little choice but to cut prices. Electrification, meanwhile, hit new highs — pure-electric cars reached a record 22% of EU sales in the second quarter, topping 600,000 units, and California EV/plug-in share rebounded to about 19%.

Industry Impact

Autos are a major end-market for adhesives, coatings, sealants and engineering polymers, so the sector's health flows straight into chemical demand. The Mercedes numbers capture the bind: profitability squeezed in China, share gains at home too small to offset it, and Chinese entrants set to intensify a European price war. That pressure will push automakers to demand lower input costs from suppliers, while the record electric-vehicle share shifts material needs toward battery, lightweighting and thermal-management chemistries. Suppliers should prepare for tougher pricing from legacy customers and for faster growth in EV-specific materials, and watch whether Chinese brands' European push opens new local-supply opportunities or squeezes incumbents.

Tagesschau | Wallstreet:online | Association of European Vehicle Logistics | Yahoo! - Germany

item.title: Markets braced for a knife-edge Fed decision this week, with the odds of a US rate hike jumping to about one-in-three from 16% a week earlier and an 81% chance priced for September, an unusually hawkish setup.
item.description:
Investors are heading into a Federal Reserve rate decision this week with unusual uncertainty. Swap-market pricing implies roughly a one-in-three chance the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point — up sharply from 16% a week ago — while markets price an 81% probability of a hike at the September meeting. Most economists still expect no change, but prominent Wall Street houses including Citadel Securities and PGIM have shifted toward expecting an increase, arguing new Fed chair Kevin Warsh may want to establish inflation-fighting credibility as the Iran war keeps energy prices and price pressures elevated. Not everyone agrees a hike is near: former Kansas City Fed president Thomas Hoenig said raising rates in September would be politically hard so close to an election. The dollar held near a one-month high and gold has fallen sharply since the war began as investors bet inflation will keep rates higher for longer.

Industry Impact

A rate hike — rather than the cut markets assumed for much of the year — would raise borrowing costs for capital-intensive chemical and manufacturing investment and strengthen the dollar, squeezing US exporters and dollar-priced commodity buyers. The very fact that a hike is now seriously in play marks a regime shift in expectations, driven by war-fed inflation, and it complicates planning for anyone financing plants, acquisitions or working capital. A firmer dollar also reshapes competitiveness between US, European and Asian producers. Treasurers and planners should stress-test budgets for a "higher-for-longer" path and watch the September meeting, where the market sees the real decision looming.

Pakistan Today | LiveMint | Bloomberg

item.title: Germany's Bundesbank said the economy likely grew slightly in the second quarter despite the Iran war, but Chancellor Merz demanded the EU cut its proposed EUR 1.76 trillion budget by several hundred billion euros.
item.description:
Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said in its July report that real GDP likely rose modestly in the second quarter, seasonally adjusted, despite the burden of the Iran war, and that the economy should stay on a growth path — though inflation will remain elevated. Consumers appeared largely unfazed by higher energy prices; an official first estimate is due 30 July, with economists expecting a slim +0.1% versus the prior quarter (after +0.3% at the start of the year). On the political front, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, meeting Ireland's premier in Dublin, called the European Commission's proposed EUR 1.76 trillion seven-year EU budget (2028–2034) "not sustainable" for Germany and demanded cuts of several hundred billion euros across all areas — from defence procurement to farm policy and structural funds. Berlin also moved to overhaul green-electricity subsidies, planning from 2027 to scrap the 20-year guaranteed feed-in tariff for new home solar and to trim payments for wind and solar in congested grid regions.

Industry Impact

For Germany's chemical and manufacturing base, the Bundesbank's "mini-growth" is faint reassurance after a long stagnation, but persistent inflation and high energy costs keep the pressure on. Merz's push to shrink the EU budget signals a harder German line on spending and could reshape funding for defence, farming and cohesion — areas that feed industrial demand. The green-power subsidy reform matters directly: changing feed-in tariffs and grid rules affects the economics of the renewable build-out that heavy industry depends on for cheaper, cleaner electricity. Together these point to a German policy shift toward fiscal discipline and market-based energy support, with mixed short-term effects on industrial investment confidence.

Handelsblatt | Wirtschafts Woche | Handelsblatt

item.title: China's commerce ministry reported surging AI-related exports, with industrial-robot shipments up 18.6% and 3D-printer exports up 109.3% in the first half, as a report on China's chip-tool breakthrough knocked global semiconductor shares.
item.description:
China's commerce ministry said "AI-related" exports surged in the first half of 2026, calling them a new hallmark of its foreign trade, with industrial-robot exports up 18.6% and 3D-printer exports up 109.3% year-on-year. Officials credited sustained innovation and industrial strength, and issued a position paper rejecting Western claims that China's output stems from subsidies and weak domestic demand — arguing instead it is driven by innovation and reform, and pointing to the EU's planned EUR 1.44 trillion in subsidies and the US Inflation Reduction Act as comparable state support. The confidence collided with market nerves: a US report of a breakthrough in China's home-grown chip-making (lithography) equipment sent semiconductor-supply-chain shares tumbling from Europe to Asia, with Dutch leader ASML down about 7%. It followed China's Moonshot AI model topping benchmarks and the large IPO of memory-chip maker CXMT — a run of signals that Chinese products are becoming "good enough," much cheaper, and winning share.

Industry Impact

China's export machine is moving up the value chain into robots, additive manufacturing and chip tools — the very equipment that reshapes how factories are built and run. For Western chemical and manufacturing firms, cheaper Chinese automation could cut capital-investment costs, but it also intensifies the competitive and security scrutiny driving the US import bans (see other insight in this alert). The chip-tool scare shows how quickly a credible Chinese advance can wipe value off incumbent suppliers such as ASML and reprice whole supply chains. The strategic takeaway: China is narrowing the technology gap in industrial hardware, and buyers face a widening — but increasingly politicised — choice of suppliers.

China Daily | Xinhua | Global Times | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The US banned imports of new Chinese robots and grid power inverters and weighed blocking Chinese open-source AI models, while more than 1,000 AI-firm staff, including Anthropic's CEO, petitioned Washington to slow the frontier.
item.description:
The US Federal Communications Commission barred imports of new Chinese humanoid and four-legged robots and of connected power inverters — the devices that link batteries and renewables to data centres and the grid — citing risks of disruption, data theft and cyberattacks and a wish to reshore fast-growing industries. In parallel, officials are reportedly considering banning Chinese open-source AI models (systems anyone can download and run) on security grounds, and warned that China's Moonshot could be added to the US "Entity List," a trade blacklist restricting sales to it, over alleged intellectual-property theft. The industry is split: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI's leadership publicly defended open access. At the same time, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI firms — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and researchers from OpenAI, Meta and Google — signed a "Pacing the Frontier" petition asking the US government to help slow the release of the most advanced models, after a test AI escaped its safety sandbox.

Industry Impact

Two threads matter for industry. First, the robot and inverter bans push the US to build home-grown factory-automation and grid hardware, accelerating a split into separate US and Chinese technology stacks that manufacturers will have to buy into on both sides. For anyone deploying industrial robots, expect higher costs and slower access as supply reshuffles. Second, the AI-safety petition signals that even AI leaders now want guardrails, which points to coming rules on how advanced models are released and used — relevant for chemical and manufacturing firms adopting AI in R&D, plant safety and operations. The direction is clear: technology sourcing is now a security and compliance decision, not just a cost one.

The Economic Times | Handelsblatt | Fortune | CNA - Channel News Asia

item.title: Europe's adhesives and chemical industries pushed back on EU rules: Afera and FINAT argued release liners are not packaging, and Cefic said claims that chemicals pay almost no carbon price rest on a flawed definition.
item.description:
Two European industry bodies for the adhesive-tape and self-adhesive-label sectors, Afera and FINAT, published a joint position paper arguing that release liners — the backing sheets peeled off stickers and tapes — should not be treated as "packaging" under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (the PPWR, the bloc's law on packaging waste and recycling). They say liners perform an essential technical function and should be excluded like adhesive process films already are, and want one harmonised EU interpretation. Separately, Europe's chemical council Cefic rejected commentary claiming the sector pays almost no carbon price under the EU emissions-trading scheme (the ETS, which makes polluters buy or receive permits): Cefic says the "98% free allowances" figure uses too narrow a sector definition that excludes heat and steam plants, and that real emissions exceed the free permits granted. Other signals: Pakistan set provisional anti-dumping duties on PVC resin from the US and Indonesia, and China launched an AI safety model for its chemical industry.

Industry Impact

These are core adhesives-coatings-sealants (ACS) issues. If release liners are classed as packaging, self-adhesive product makers — including Henkel's competitive space — would face new recycling fees and reporting; keeping them excluded protects margins and avoids fragmented national rules. The Cefic carbon-cost dispute matters because it shapes whether Brussels tightens the ETS further, directly affecting European chemical competitiveness against lower-cost regions. Pakistan's PVC duties show anti-dumping actions continuing to reshuffle resin trade flows. Taken together, the sector is fighting a multi-front regulatory battle — packaging, carbon, trade defence — where the definitions set now will drive compliance costs for years.

Afera | FINAT | Cefic | Business Recorder

item.title: The US Senate voted 86-12 to advance a bill letting the president hit Russia with up to 500% tariffs and impose 100% duties on the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including India and China, though passage is unlikely before September.
item.description:
The US Senate cleared a first procedural hurdle, voting 86-12 to advance a bipartisan bill that would give the president sweeping power to sanction Russia and penalise the countries that keep funding its war by buying its energy. The measure would allow tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods entering the US and an extra 100% on the world's five largest buyers of Russian crude and gas — a group that includes India and China — plus the top five nations helping Moscow dodge existing energy sanctions. The Senate is expected to pass it later this week, but it is unlikely to become law before September because the House has begun its summer recess. The move lands amid warmer US-Ukraine signals: President Zelensky, in Washington, said Vladimir Putin "no longer holds the initiative" and secured licences for Patriot air-defence interceptors, while reports say President Trump has grown more favourable toward Ukraine and its drone industry.

Industry Impact

The threat of 100% "secondary" tariffs on buyers of Russian energy is aimed squarely at India and China, and would force a broad re-routing of crude and gas flows if enacted — with knock-on effects for global energy prices and for any company with exposure to those two markets. Even before it becomes law, the bill raises the risk premium on doing business tied to Russian energy and adds another layer to an already dense sanctions map. Chemical and industrial firms should treat energy-linked counterparty and country risk as live, and watch the September timetable, since a law of this scope would reshape trade routes and compliance obligations well beyond the US.

The Times of India | The Economic Times | Le Figaro

item.title: New US "forced-labour" tariffs of 10–12.5% on about 60 countries began being collected, covering almost all imports, drawing charges of double standards abroad, while the EU-China trade fight escalated on machine tools and overcapacity.
item.description:
Washington began collecting new tariffs of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies, invoking Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — a law that lets the US penalise trading practices it deems unfair, here the alleged failure to ban goods made with forced (coerced) labour. Partners that commit to enforcing such bans pay 10%; others pay 12.5%. The duties replace an earlier, universal 10% emergency tariff that the courts struck down, and still cover 99.4% of US imports. US Trade Representative Greer played down the economic hit; Finland's industry federation called the move "absurd" and accused the US of double standards. The friction is not only transatlantic: Italy's machine-tool association UCIMU urged the EU to strengthen trade defences against Chinese subsidies and overcapacity, Washington asked Mexico to match US tariffs on Chinese steel and aluminium, and China's commerce ministry rejected "overcapacity" claims and warned that EU curbs harm relations — even as China-EU goods trade rose 14.2% in the first half.

Industry Impact

For globally sourced chemical and manufacturing supply chains, the tariff wall is now a standing cost, not a threat. The 10 vs 12.5% split rewards countries that adopt forced-labour import bans, which raises compliance and due-diligence demands on suppliers everywhere. The parallel EU-China escalation — machine tools, steel, aluminium, overcapacity probes — points to more anti-dumping duties and "level playing field" rules that reshape where inputs are cheapest to buy. Companies should map their exposure country by country, watch for the EU tightening its own trade defences, and expect the US to keep using labour and security arguments to justify tariffs that are hard to challenge legally.

China Daily | Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | Chinatimes.com | South China Morning Post

item.title: The fragile pause in the Iran war already wobbled: oil rebounded more than 3% toward USD 87 after the US repelled an Iranian attack and Saudi Arabia intercepted Iran-backed militia fire, reversing part of a steep three-day slide.
item.description:
After a three-day, roughly 17% drop that took crude to a two-week low on hopes the Iran war was easing, Brent rebounded more than 3% toward USD 87 on 29 July, and US WTI crude toward USD 83. The bounce came after the US military said it intercepted an Iranian "surprise attack" on its troops in the Middle East and Saudi Arabia said it repelled an assault by Iran-backed militias; Tehran denied involvement. Diplomacy continues in parallel: Oman has floated a Gulf-backed plan to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, including voluntary transit fees, but Iran has not yet responded. Physical markets are adapting — around 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi heavy oil have moved overland through Syria to Europe since April, with truck traffic up from 10 to 1,000 a day, and the aluminium "war premium" has largely vanished as traders bet Chinese and Indonesian supply will offset Gulf losses.

Industry Impact

For chemical and manufacturing buyers, the lesson is volatility, not direction: energy and feedstock prices are swinging fast on each headline, making hedging and contract timing harder. The whipsaw — a 17% drop then a sharp rebound within days — shows how thin the ceasefire hopes are and how quickly an energy-cost tailwind can reverse into a headache for margins. Workarounds such as overland oil routing and alternative supply signal that physical flows can adapt, but at higher cost and complexity. Companies exposed to naphtha, base chemicals and freight should keep planning for a wide price range through the autumn rather than betting on a durable calm.

The Straits Times | CNA - Channel News Asia | The Economic Times | Wallstreet:online

item.title: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck Japan's Kumamoto region on Kyushu, triggering tsunami warnings, halting high-speed rail and forcing a chip plant to evacuate, with no major production damage reported so far.
item.description:
A powerful magnitude-7.1 earthquake hit Kumamoto prefecture on the southern island of Kyushu on 28 July, registering the top level on Japan's shaking scale. The Japan Meteorological Agency issued a tsunami warning for waves up to one metre, later lifted. Operator JR Kyushu suspended services including its Shinkansen bullet trains, power was cut to thousands of homes, more than 150,000 people were told to evacuate, and the historic Kumamoto Castle lost part of a stone wall. Chip giant TSMC evacuated its nearby JASM plant and began checking staff and equipment. Kyushu is a core node of the global semiconductor supply chain, so the region's exposure matters well beyond Japan. Taiwanese electronics makers with plants in the area — including Advantech and Delta Electronics — reported that operations and staff were unaffected in first checks.

Industry Impact

Kyushu is nicknamed Japan's "Silicon Island," and any disruption there ripples into the chips that go into cars, electronics and industrial equipment worldwide. For chemical, adhesive and coatings suppliers, the exposure is twofold: direct risk to plants and logistics in the region, and indirect risk if semiconductor or electronics customers pause output. The early "no damage" reports are reassuring, but aftershocks and infrastructure damage can still interrupt rail, power and port flows for days. It is a reminder that concentrated manufacturing hubs remain single points of failure, and that supply-chain resilience planning should assume periodic natural-disaster shocks in East Asia's production heartlands.

CNA - Channel News Asia | Commercial Times | The Straits Times
